title: From Buc-ee's to BBQ: World Cup Tourists Find Unexpected Joy in Everyday America
summary: When Rinta Goto bit into the bread at a Texas Roadhouse in Dallas, he wasn't expecting a life-changing experience. But the 24-year-old Japanese tourist was so blown away that he posted about the "insanely good" bread and "ridiculously delicious" steak—and over 200,000 people took notice. Goto, in the U.S. for the World Cup, also marveled at free soda refills at McDonald's, a massive Starbucks, and Walmart's family-sized bags of Reese's. When he learned Texas Roadhouse has locations in several countries—but not Japan—he dropped his head in his hands. "Why isn't Japan on the list?" he asked in anguish. Goto is part of a wave of international soccer fans flooding social media with their discoveries of everyday America. They're gushing over yellow school buses, Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders, sunburns on supposedly rainy days, and the mega convenience store Buc-ee's. Even Spanish soccer star Lamine Yamal made a Walmart pit stop. This enthusiasm comes at a diplomatically tense moment. The U.S. has strained relationships with many overseas allies, and its immigration policies have complicated the tournament—at least one referee and a team staffer were denied entry, along with fans who couldn't get visas. Yet experts say the organic appreciation of American culture is a powerful form of soft power. "At a time when there is so much criticism and uncertainty with regard to the United States, for our country to have this unexpected windfall of people from around the world coming to the U.S. and seeing the real aspects of everyday America... It's just an unexpected fringe benefit beyond the sports itself," said Victor Cha, president of geopolitics and foreign policy at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Not everyone is convinced the posts are genuine—some question whether the celebration is authentic. But for fans like Kanna Matsuda, another Japanese visitor, the experience was real. She was pleasantly surprised by her huge Airbnb in Dallas. "That was a big house. I loved that," she said. She plans to return after watching games in Mexico, uttering words she never expected: "I'm excited to go back again to Dallas." In Kansas City, English fan George Elek and his friends fell hard for the city in just two days. They tried burnt ends, ribs, and mac and cheese from a gas station restaurant, navigated the Kansas-Missouri divide, and carefully avoided the barbecue war between Kansas City and Texas. "I just hadn't prepared myself for how much we would be wowed by Kansas City, and the people, and the vibe," Elek said. They even considered returning just for the restaurants and people—no soccer required.
why_it_matters: This story shows how everyday encounters can reshape a country's image, even when governments disagree—and when you share your own experiences online, you might influence how the world sees your home.

background_read: The FIFA World Cup is the world's most watched sporting event, held every four years; the 2026 edition is co-hosted by the USA, Canada, and Mexico, drawing millions of visitors.

Soft power is a term coined by political scientist Joseph Nye to describe a country's ability to attract others through its culture, values, and everyday life rather than through military or economic force.
Victor Cha, an expert on geopolitics, is from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a well-known Washington D.C. think tank that studies global security and policy.

During major events, tourists often post on social media about ordinary things they find exciting—this can unintentionally shape how a country is viewed abroad, especially when official government relations are tense.
Lamine Yamal, the Spanish soccer star mentioned, is a teenage phenomenon who became FC Barcelona's youngest ever scorer at age 15 and already represents Spain in the World Cup.

perspectives.perspective: Positive: Tourism boost and cultural exchange
perspectives.description: Local businesses, from restaurants to convenience stores, gain unexpected customers and worldwide free publicity. Tourists leave with joyful memories, potentially returning or encouraging others to visit, strengthening people-to-people ties.

The U.S. immigration system blocked some World Cup staff and fans, so the glowing social media stories don't represent everyone. Critics might also argue that brief consumer experiences don't erase deeper political disagreements or unfair global perceptions.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral: The mechanics of soft power
perspectives.description: This is a real-time example of soft power—when ordinary life attracts foreign admiration without government planning. The pattern isn't new: during past Olympics or World Cups, visitors' positive impressions sometimes temporarily improved a host's global reputation.

The World Cup could be a model for how big events build bridges. Future hosts might encourage similar everyday discoveries, but they must also ensure fair visa processes and learn from the authenticity debate—forced positivity can backfire.
